Linear classifiers like logistic regression or SVMs often struggle with generalization when handling large output spaces where some classes have very few examples [P2_p1_c04]. While deep learning or low-rank matrix factorization solve this, they can be slow [P2_p1_c02][P2_p1_c04]. This paper introduces fastText, a fast and efficient baseline for text and sentence classification [P2_p1_c02][P2_p1_c04].

The architecture uses a rank constraint where a first weight matrix $A$ acts as a look-up table over words [P2_p1_c04]. These word representations are averaged into a text representation, which is then fed to a linear classifier [P2_p1_c04]. To capture local word order without high computational costs, fastText uses a bag of n-grams as additional features, maintaining a memory-efficient mapping through the hashing trick [P2_p2_c03].

In sentiment analysis experiments, fastText achieves accuracy slightly better than char-CNN and char-CRNN, and is competitive with recurrent approaches like LSTM-GRNN, without using pre-trained word embeddings [P2_p3_c02]. Furthermore, adding bigram information improves performance by 1% to 4% [P2_p3_c02]. For scalability, evaluated on a tag prediction task using the YFCC100M dataset with 91,188,648 training examples and 312,116 unique tags, fastText trains on more than one billion words in less than ten minutes on a standard multicore CPU [P2_p1_c02][P2_p4_c02]. It can also classify half a million sentences among 312K classes in less than a minute [P2_p1_c02].
